# Mahāgopālaka Sutta (MN 33 (PTS MN i 220))

**ID:** MN 33 (PTS MN i 220)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāgopālaka Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Longer Discourse on the Cowherd
**PTS:** MN i 220
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn33
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāgopālaka Sutta* (MN 33) is set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, where the Buddha addresses the monks with an extended pastoral simile [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse enumerates eleven failings that prevent a cowherd from properly tending his herd, comparing them to eleven detrimental qualities that hinder a mendicant's spiritual growth; conversely, eleven positive qualities are taught that foster growth and maturity in the Dhamma [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Among the required skills of a monk is knowing the proper pasture, an image that signifies the contemplation of *satipaṭṭhāna* [Analayo 2006; Analayo 2010]. Another crucial factor is approaching experienced elder monks who preserve the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the *mātṛkā*s (*mātikā*) to question them and resolve interpretive perplexities [Analayo, Dawn of Abhidharma; Nance, Sūtra comm lit diss]. Drawing attention to the emphasis placed on venerating senior elders (*theras*), G. C. Pande considers this textual feature an indicator of the sutta's relatively late institutional composition [Pande 1974]. Dan Lusthaus further notes thematic affinities between this discourse and the *Pratītyasamutpādavibhaṅganirdeśasūtra* [Lusthaus 2002].

MN 33 shares an almost identical Pali parallel in the Aṅguttaranikāya (AN 11.17) [SuttaCentral; Donner 1976; Lamotte, Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra]. Automatic analysis by DharmaNexus confirms this close Pali-internal relationship, identifying extensive reuse between MN 33 (§2.1–27.6) and AN 11.17 (§17.0.3–17.28.1) at 0.97 similarity, alongside stock doctrinal passages shared with AN 4, AN 5, AN 3, and SN 35 [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Pali canon, parallels to the cowherd rules are attested in Chinese Āgamas, notably in Kumārajīva's translation *Fangniu jing* (T 123), the *Ekottarāgama* (EĀ 49.1 / T 125), and the *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 1249 / T 99), as well as Sanskrit fragments, the Tibetan *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* (D 6 / D 211), and Mahāyāna treatises such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra* (T 1509) and Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Donner 1976; Lamotte, Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra]. Anālayo points out that where MN 33 refers to learned monks who preserve the *mātṛkā*s, its *Saṃyuktāgama* parallel mentions the *Abhidharma*, reflecting early terminological developments between the early discourse and Vinaya traditions [Analayo, Dawn of Abhidharma].
